1. Intro to Microeconomics

First steps in microeconomics — no calculus, learn by touching sliders. From gasoline prices and lunch menus to cafes, subscriptions, and cigarette taxes: see the logic behind everyday choices.

  • Where Demand Meets Supply — Touch why a liter of gasoline costs what it costs. Quantity demanded Qd=a−bPQ_d = a - bPQd​=a−bP falls as price rises; quantity supplied Qs=dPQ_s = dPQs​=dP rises. The point where the two match — Qd=QsQ_d = Q_sQd​=Qs​ — is the equilibrium.
  • Splitting the Lunch Budget — Split a 404040 lunch budget between two foods. The money constraint is one line: p1x1+p2x2=mp_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = mp1​x1​+p2​x2​=m. The best combo is where the last won buys the same happiness everywhere — raise a price and watch that point slide.
  • The Cafe Owner's Math — You run a cafe. The cost of one more cup is MC=ΔC/ΔqMC = \Delta C / \Delta qMC=ΔC/Δq — rising with every cup. While the price PPP beats that cost, selling pays; stopping at P=MCP = MCP=MC is the answer.
  • Competition vs Monopoly — The same streaming market, side by side: competition left, monopoly right. The monopolist stops at MR=MCMR = MCMR=MC, and the lost triangle (deadweight loss) glows red. Lower the demand responsiveness and the red triangle grows — insensitive customers hurt more.
  • Taxes and Price Ceilings — Who pays a 333 cigarette tax? The tax wedge Pb=Ps+tP_b = P_s + tPb​=Ps​+t lands heavier on the side that cannot walk away. A rent ceiling, meanwhile, freezes the price but creates a queue. Push the sliders and see for yourself.
  • Two Firms Watching Each Other — A town with only two cola firms. The price is set by their combined output: P=a−b(q1+q2)P = a - b(q_1 + q_2)P=a−b(q1​+q2​). Once the rival picks q2q_2q2​, your best move comes from the reply rule q1=a−c−bq22bq_1 = \frac{a - c - b q_2}{2b}q1​=2ba−c−bq2​​. The market settles where the two replies cross.
  • The Factory and the River — A factory dumps waste in a river, and the fishing village downstream pays for it. The factory's cost MPCMPCMPC plus the river's damage MDMDMD is society's true cost, MSC=MPC+MDMSC = MPC + MDMSC=MPC+MD. The market hears only MPCMPCMPC and makes too much — the right tax closes the gap.
  • Tragedy of the Shared Pasture — The pasture belongs to everyone; the sheep belong to each herder. A sheep's worth v(S)=a−bSv(S) = a - bSv(S)=a−bS falls as the total flock SSS grows, yet each herder counts only their own animals. The more herders share the field, the further the total overshoots the optimum — and the pasture's profit evaporates.
  • Why Does the Superstar Earn So Much? — A star singer's fee and land by a new station split the same way. Of the payment www for a factor, what it could earn elsewhere is transfer earnings; the pure bonus on top is economic rent. The steeper the supply w=c+sqw = c + sqw=c+sq — the harder the factor is to replace — the more of the payment hardens into rent.
  • The Amusement Park Pricing Puzzle — There are three ways to sell the same ride. Per-ride pricing charges like a monopolist, a flat pass makes extra rides free and invites overuse, and a two-part tariff splits the bill into two pieces, F+pqF + pqF+pq. Price rides at cost and collect the surplus at the gate, and the waste vanishes — but so does the guest's share.
  • Three Ways to Tax — One market, three taxes. A lump-sum bill LLL never enters the price decision and leaves trade untouched, a specific tax ttt drives a fixed wedge per unit, and an ad valorem tax τ\tauτ stretches the buyer's price to (1+τ)(1 + \tau)(1+τ) times the seller's. Only wedged taxes shrink trade and leave a triangle behind.
